definition: In the bin covering problem, items of different sizes must be packed into a finite number of bins or containers, each of which must contain at least a certain given total size, in a way that maximizes the number of bins used.
details: This problem is a dual of the bin packing problem: in bin covering, the bin sizes are bounded from below and the goal is to maximize their number; in bin packing, the bin sizes are bounded from above and the goal is to minimize their number. The problem is NP-hard, but there are various efficient approximation algorithms: Algorithms covering at least 1/2, 2/3 or 3/4 of the optimum bin count asymptotically, running in time O ( n ) , O ( n log ⁡ n ) , O ( n log 2 n ) {\displaystyle O(n),O(n\log n),O(n{\log }^{2}n)} respectively. An asymptotic PTAS, algorithms with bounded worst-case behavior whose expected behavior is asymptotically-optimal for some discrete distributions, and a learning algorithm with asymptotically optimal expected behavior for all discrete distributions. An asymptotic FPTAS.

explainer.lead: Bin covering asks how to split items of different sizes into as many groups as possible while giving every group at least a required total size. It reverses the usual packing goal: instead of fitting everything into as few bins as possible, you try to fill as many bins as possible to the minimum level.

tiers.eli5: Imagine you have a pile of snacks and lots of lunch bags, and every bag must get at least a handful; you want to fill as many bags as possible.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use approximation algorithms, since the problem is NP-hard, and a common pitfall is confusing it with bin packing and optimising the wrong direction.
tiers.paperLevel: Pack items into a finite number of bins so each bin's total size is at least a given bound, maximising the number of bins used; it is the dual of bin packing and is NP-hard, but approximations cover at least 1/2, 2/3 or 3/4 of the optimum asymptotically in O(n), O(n log n) and O(n log^2 n) time.

explainer.example: With item sizes 6, 5, 4, and 5 and a bin threshold of 10, pack 6+4 into one bin and 5+5 into another. Both bins reach 10, and three bins are impossible because the total item size is only 20, below the required 30.
explainer.intuition: The challenge is to avoid overfilling early bins: items saved from one bin may provide the threshold for another. Since every bin needs a minimum total size, the best arrangement spreads the available size across the largest feasible number of bins.
howItWorks: Start with item sizes and a minimum total size required for each covered bin.
Group items so every bin you count reaches that threshold.
Avoid placing more items in a bin when they could help complete another bin.
Choose a feasible grouping that maximizes the number of covered bins.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a precise optimization model for situations where outputs must meet a lower bound and the goal is to produce as many qualifying outputs as possible. Its hardness also makes approximation quality and running time central parts of the problem.
misconceptions: It is not ordinary bin packing: bin covering maximizes bins with lower-bounded loads, while bin packing minimizes bins with upper-bounded loads.
Filling one bin as much as possible can be counterproductive because excess items may be needed to cover another bin.
